div.head: Background
div.p: The Hippo pathway is a conserved tumour suppressor signalling pathway, and its dysregulation is often associated with abnormal cell growth and tumorigenesis. We previously revealed that the transcriptional coactivator Yes-associated protein (YAP), the key effector of the Hippo pathway, is a molecular target for glioblastoma (GBM), the most common malignant brain tumour. Inhibiting YAP with small interfering RNA (siYAP) or the specific inhibitor verteporfin (VP) can diminish GBM growth to a certain degree.

div.head: Results
div.p: In this study, to enhance the anti-GBM effect of siYAP and VP, we designed stepwise-targeting and hypoxiaresponsive liposomes (AMVY@NPs), which encapsulate hypoxia-responsive polymetronidazole-coated VP and DOTAP adsorbed siYAP, with angiopep-2 (A2) modification on the surface. AMVY@NPs exhibited excellent blood-brain barrier crossing, GBM targeting, and hypoxia-responsive and efficient siYAP and VP release properties. By inhibiting the expression and function of YAP, AMVY@NPs synergistically inhibited both the growth and stemness of GBM in vitro. Moreover, AMVY@NPs strongly inhibited the growth of orthotopic U87 xenografts and improved the survival of tumour-bearing mice without adverse effects.

Conclusion Specific targeting of YAP with stepwise-targeting and hypoxia-responsive liposome AMVY@NPs carrying siYAP and VP efficiently inhibited GBM progression. This study provides a valuable drug delivery platform and creative insights for molecular targeted treatment of GBM in the future.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common primary malignant tumour in the brain and has a high recurrence rate, high mortality rate, and poor prognosis [1,2]. Moreover, despite comprehensive treatment, including surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy, the 5-year survival rate of GBM patients remains below 5% [3]. erefore, finding new methods to treat GBM and improve the survival outcome of patients is important. Molecular targeted therapy is a trending hot spot of tumour therapy research [4], and many key molecular targets have been identified in GBM, providing new options for GBM treatment.

Hippo signalling is a protein kinase pathway that controls organ size and tissue homeostasis by regulating cell growth and proliferation [5,6]. Recently, numerous studies have revealed that the Hippo pathway is dysregulated in a variety of tumours, leading to overactivation of the transcriptional coactivator Yes-associated protein (YAP), the main effector of the Hippo pathway.

e overactivation of YAP preserves the stemness of tumour stem cells, promotes the growth of tumour cells and inhibits tumour immunity, resulting in the malignant progression of tumours. In our previous study, we reported that YAP is highly expressed in gliomas and is associated with the poor prognosis of glioma patients [7,8]. YAP promotes the malignant progression of glioma through various mechanisms [8][9][10][11]. Our studies revealed that YAP is a key molecular therapeutic target for GBM and that downregulation of YAP via small interfering RNA (siRNA) inhibits GBM progression [9], suggesting potential clinical application value.

In addition, because YAP must be translocated into the nucleus to bind to the transcription factor TEA domain transcription factor (TEAD) and then promote the transcription of its target genes, blocking the binding of YAP to TEAD is also one of the main strategies used to inhibit YAP activity [12]. Verteporfin (VP) is a porphyrin photosensitizer used for the clinical treatment of neovascular macular degeneration. Many studies have reported that nonphotoactivated VP inhibits tumour proliferation by blocking the YAP-TEAD interaction and inhibiting YAP expression to reduce its transcriptional activity [13,14].

We previously reported that siYAP or VP alone could partially inhibit GBM growth [10,11], and we wanted to completely block the growth of GBM with the combination of siYAP and VP in this study. However, the poor stability of siRNAs under physiological conditions and their inability to cross the cellular membrane remain the major roadblocks for the use of siRNAs in GBM treatments [15]. In addition, VP is a hydrophobic macromolecule, which has difficulty penetrating the blood-brain barrier (BBB) [16,17]. erefore, there is an urgent need to overcome the above obstacles for delivering siYAP and VP into gliomas, thereby inhibiting YAP to diminish glioma progression.

Nanomedicine, which is considered an emerging vehicle in the field of cancer therapy, can overcome the above obstacles [18] and increase the concentration of drugs in gliomas [19,20]. Various nanocarriers have been designed to deliver drugs for cancer-targeted therapy [21,22], such as liposomes and micelles [23,24], among which cationic lipids are the most widely used in the systemic delivery of siRNA via electrostatic adsorption to protect the siRNA from degradation by serum nucleases [25,26]. Additionally, hypoxia is a salient feature of solid tumours, and the partial pressure of oxygen is near 0 mmHg in GBM, whereas it is approximately 30 mmHg in normal tissues [27,28]. Our laboratory demonstrated that polymetronidazole can form a hydrophobic core to enclose poorly water-soluble drugs and that the nitro group of nitroimidazoles can be converted to an amino group through a series of selective bioreductions to release the drug cargo under hypoxic conditions [29].

In this study, we developed a cationic liposome with a hypoxic response (Fig. 1), which consisted of three functional moieties. (1) Polymetronidazole formed a hydrophobic core to encapsulate VP, a poorly water-soluble drug. (2) siYAP was loaded onto the cationic material DOTAP by electrostatic adsorption, which enveloped the polymetronidazole matrix core. Moreover, DSPE-PEG 2000 was used to stabilize the structures that combined with liposomes via covalent bonding. (3) DSPE-PEG 2000 -conjugated Angiopep-2 (A2) was attached to the surface, which can target low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1), which is highly expressed in GBM [30][31][32]. We called these cationic liposomes AMVY@NPs (A: Angiopep-2; M: polymetronidazole; V: VP; Y: siYAP). In our study, after GBM was targeted via the A2-LRP1 interaction, AMVY@NPs could responsively release siYAP and VP in the hypoxic microenvironment. siYAP and VP synergistically inhibited the expression and function of YAP to diminish GBM progression.

div.head: Materials and methods
div.p: Cell culture e glioma cell lines U87 and U251, normal human astrocyte HA1800 and mouse brain microvascular endothelial bEnd.3 were purchased from the Shanghai Cell Bank, Chinese Academy of Sciences. All of the cells were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium ( ermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) supplemented with 10% foetal bovine serum ( ermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). Primary GBM and glioma stem cells (GSCs) were extracted from glioma specimens obtained from the Department of Neurosurgery at the Affiliated Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University.

div.head: Antibodies and reagents
div.p: Rabbit monoclonal anti-YAP, mouse monoclonal anti-βactin and rabbit monoclonal anti-CD133 antibodies were obtained from Abcam. Mouse monoclonal anti-CTGF was obtained from Santa Cruz. Rabbit monoclonal anti-AXL was obtained from CST. Mouse monoclonal anti-Nestin was obtained from Millipore.

Polymetronidazole was purchased from Xi'an Ruixi Biological Tech. and characterized by nuclear magnetic and gel permeation chromatography (Figure S1). Poly(d, l-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Verteporfin was obtained from MedChem-Express (MCE), and its chemical structure was shown in Figure S2A. 1,2-Dioleoyl-3-trimethylammoniumpropane (DOTAP) was obtained from Corden Pharma. DSPE-PEG2000 was obtained from Aladdin. Angiopep-2 was obtained from GL Biochem (Shanghai) Ltd. Lecithin was obtained from AVT (Shanghai) Pharmaceutical Tech.

div.head: Preparation and characterization of AMVY@NPs
div.p: DOTAP (1 mg), polymetronidazole (0.3 mg), DSPE-PEG 2000 (0.3 mg), DSPE-PEG2000-A2 (0.2 mg), lecithin (0.1 mg) and VP (0.1 mg) were completely solubilized in DMSO. siYAP (0.025 mg) was dissolved in DEPC water. VP was encapsulated with polymetronidazole by gently stirring for 5 min. en, siYAP was loaded onto the cationic material DOTAP by electrostatic adsorption, which enveloped the polymetronidazole matrix core during gentle stirring for 5 min. DSPE-PEG 2000 and A2-conjugated DSPE-PEG 2000 were added to the above materials. e mixtures were vortexed vigorously for 2 min and then added to water under vigorous stirring for 20 min, followed by gentle stirring for 2 h at room temperature to Fig. 1 Schematic representation of the AMVY@NPs formation and delivery system A AMVY@NPs were formulated by angiopep-2 (A2), polymetronidazole (M), Veterporfin (V), siYAP (Y), DOTAP, lecithin and DSPE-PEG2000. AMVY@NPs responsively release siYAP and VP in hypoxic conditions. B After tail vein injection, AMVY@NPs crossed the BBB and targeted into GBM. C Based on the hypoxia-responsive properties of polymetronidazole, AMVY@NPs disintegrated in hypoxic glioma cells and released siYAP and VP, which inhibited YAP expression and function, leading to a synergistic inhibiting effect on glioma growth form A2-modified cationic lipid nanoparticles (AMVY@ NPs). ereafter, the AMVY@NPs were purified by dialysis against phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.40) for 12 h to remove the DMSO.
e APVY@NPs control group was prepared in the same way as above except that the polymetronidazole was replaced with PLGA.
e nanoparticle size and zeta potential were measured using a Zetasizer (ZS-90/Malvern).
e morphology and size of the nanoparticles were observed with transmission electron microscopy (TEM).

div.head: Encapsulation efficiency (EE) of VP
div.p: After dialysis, the dialysate solution was collected and tested via a multifunctional microplate reader (detection at 450 nm) to obtain the amount of free VP. e amount of encapsulated VP was calculated by subtracting the amount of free VP from the amount of total VP used to prepare the AMVY@NPs. ereafter, the encapsulation efficiency (inclusion rate) was calculated by dividing the amount of total VP used to prepare the AMVY@NPs by the amount of encapsulated VP.

div.head: EE =
div.p: Amount of VP in total -Amount of free VP tested Amount of VP in total × 100%

div.head: Gel retardation assay
div.p: e ability of AMVY@NPs to load siYAP was measured by a gel retardation assay.

e amount of siYAP in the AMVY@NPs was determined by the gradient N/P ratio of DOTAP to siYAP. Heparin sodium (1000 units/mL) was used to inhibit siYAP binding with AMVY@NPs by competitively adsorbing on the surface of liposomes through electrostatic action [33].

div.head: Release of VP and siYAP
div.p: e release of VP and siYAP (modified with Cy5) from AMVY@NPs or APVY@NPs was detected under hypoxic and normoxic environments via a dialysis method. One millilitre of AMVY@NPs or APVY@NPs was added to a dialysis bag (MWCO 3500 kDa for VP, MWCO 12000-14000 kDa for siYAP), which was then sealed tightly and put into a tube with 30 mL of PBS. e tube was shaken well at 100 rpm in a constant temperature shaker at 37 °C. One millilitre of PBS was removed at different time points, and the same volume of PBS was added to the dialysis bag. e contents of released VP and Cy5-siYAP were detected via a multifunctional microplate reader.

In Vitro Hypoxia-responsive Ability e normoxic or hypoxic microenvironment was simulated by using a normoxic incubator or three-gas incubator (O 2 2%, CO 2 5%, N 2 93%) at 37 °C. e nitro group in polymetronidazole has a characteristic absorption peak at 325 nm. When hydrophobic 2-nitroimidazole was converted into hydrophilic 2-aminoimidazole through a series of selective bioreduction reactions under low-oxygen conditions, the absorption peak of polymetronidazole at 325 nm disappeared. erefore, taking advantage of this principle, we examined the hypoxia response of polymetronidazole by testing the characteristic absorption peak at 325 nm with a multifunctional microplate reader. In addition, the diameter and morphology of the AMVY@NPs were detected via Zetasizer and transmission electron microscopy (TEM), respectively.

In Vitro Material Cytotoxicity HA1800, U87, U251 and GBM cells were seeded in 96-well plates at 5 × 10 3 cells/well. Twenty-four hours later, the cells were treated with nanoparticles (without VP or siYAP) for 24 h. e cell viability was measured by a CCK-8 assay to assess the toxicity of the packaging material.

div.head: In Vitro BBB Crossing Ability
div.p: e in vitro BBB model was established via a Transwell assay. e upper chamber of the 24-well plate was filled with 10 × 10 4 mixed bEnd.3 and HA1800 cells. e lower chamber was seeded with 5 × 10 4 U87 cells and cultured for 24 h. ereafter, drugs were added to the upper chamber. Four hours later, U87 cells were fixed with 4% PFA and stained with DAPI. e ability of the nanoparticles to cross the BBB was reflected by Cy5-siYAP fluorescence.

div.head: Lysosome escape of AMVY@NPs
div.p: LysoTracker Green was obtained from Beyotime. U87 cells were plated into 24-well plates at 2 × 10 4 cells/ well and cultured for 24 h. ereafter, AMCy5-siYAP@ NPs were added to the wells, and the lysosomes were stained with LysoTracker at 0 h, 4 h, and 8 h after incubation in a three-gas incubator. e U87 cells were fixed with 4% PFA and stained with DAPI. Photographs were acquired using laser confocal microscopy, and the localization of lysosomes and Cy5-siYAP was visualized via fluorescence.

div.head: Western blotting analysis
div.p: Equal amounts of protein were separated and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride membranes with a 0.45 μm pore size (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA). e membrane was subsequently probed with primary antibodies and secondary antibodies.

ereafter, the bound antibodies were detected by an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) detection system ( ermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). Band densities were quantified by using Image-Pro Plus Software (Media Cybernetics, Inc., Rockville, MD, USA).

div.head: Quantitative real-time PCR
div.p: Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA), and cDNA was prepared via a first-strand cDNA kit (Tiangen Biotech) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
e primers used were generated by Suzhou Biosyntech, and the sequences used were as follows:

div.head: CCK-8 assay
div.p: A Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) was purchased from ApexBio. U87 and U251 cells were seeded at 5 × 10 3 cells/ well into 96-well plates and cultured. Twenty-four hours later, the cells were treated with drugs under hypoxia for 8 h and then cultured under normoxia with fresh medium without drugs for 24 h. ereafter, the cell viability was measured via a CCK-8 assay according to the manufacturer's instructions.

div.head: Colony formation assay
div.p: U251 cells were plated in six-well plates at 500 cells/well and incubated for 24 h. ereafter, the cells were treated with drugs and cultured under hypoxia for 8 h. Later, the cells were incubated under normoxia for 21 days to grow colonies, and the medium was changed every seven days.
e cells were then fixed with 4% PFA for 1 h and stained overnight with a crystal violet dye.

Live/dead cell assay U251 cells were plated at 10 × 10 4 /well in a 96-well plate for 24 h. ereafter, the cells were treated with drugs and cultured under hypoxia for 8 h. Later, the cells were incubated under normoxia for 24 h in fresh medium and then stained with an AM/PI Cell Viability/Cytotoxicity Kit (KeyGEN BioTECH) according to the manufacturer's instructions.

div.head: Extraction and culturing of glioma stem cells (GSCs)
div.p: e glioma samples were obtained from the Department of Neurosurgery at the Affiliated Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University. GSCs were isolated from surgical specimens via mechanical and enzymatic dissociation and cultured in serum-free medium for free-floating spheroid formation as previously described [34]. e F12 medium ( ermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) was supplemented with 1 mL of B27 ( ermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.), 500 µL of N2 ( ermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.), 20 ng/µL of FGF2 (PeproTech, Inc.) and 20 ng/µL of EGF (PeproTech, Inc.). e GSCs were dissociated using accutase (Sigma) to create a single-cell suspension prior to seeding.

div.head: Sphere formation assay
div.p: e sphere formation assay was performed as previously described [35]. GSCs were seeded at 1000 cells/well in a 96-well plate. GSCs were treated with drugs under hypoxia for 8 h.
en, the GSCs were incubated under normoxia. Fourteen days after seeding, the number of spheres formed by the GSCs was determined.

div.head: Limited dilution assay
div.p: e limited dilution assay was performed as previously described [36]. To perform descending dilutions, GSCs at concentrations of 160, 80, 40, 20, 10 and 5 cells/well were seeded in 96-well plates. ereafter, the cells were treated with drugs for 8 h under hypoxia and then incubated under normoxia. e number of GSCs was assessed 14 days after seeding via extreme limiting dilution analysis (ELDA) software ( h t t p : / / b i o i n f . w e h i . e d u . a u / s o f t w a r e / e l d a; [37]).

div.head: Orthotopic glioma model in nude mice
div.p: BALB/c nude mice (6-8 weeks, 20-25 g) were obtained from Gempharmatech Company (Nanjing, China). All animal experiments were approved by the Xuzhou Medical University of China Animal Care and Use Committee (Ethics identifier: 202205A378).

e orthotopic glioma model was established in nude mice according to our previous study [11]. Briefly, U87-GFP-Luci + cells in 5 µL of Leibovitz's L-15 medium ( ermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) were injected into the right striatum of the mice (n ≥ 6 per group). Seven days after tumour cell transplantation, the nude mice were monitored by in vivo bioluminescence imaging to confirm whether the orthotopic glioma model was successfully established.

div.head: Cy5-siYAP concentration-fluorescence curve
div.p: e fluorescence of Cy5-conjugated siYAP (Cy5-siYAP) was detected at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, and 10 µg/mL under a fluorescence intensity of 660 nm. A concentration-fluorescence curve was drawn according to the results.

div.head: In VivoBBB penetration and intratumoral distribution
div.p: After the orthotopic glioma model was successfully established, drugs were administered to the glioma-bearing mice via the tail vein. ereafter, the fluorescence of Cy5-siYAP was examined at 0 h, 1 h, 2 h, 4 h, 8 h, 12 h and 24 h after injection. Blood samples were collected to measure the fluorescence intensity of Cy5-siYAP via a multifunctional microplate reader. At 4 h after drug injection, three mice from each group were euthanized.

e fluorescence of Cy5-siYAP in the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys and brain of each mouse was measured with an IVIS imaging system. e brains were prepared into frozen slices to observe the distribution of Cy5-siYAP in the xenografts.

div.head: Assay of the hypoxia condition in GBM tissues
div.p: Hypoxic conditions in the xenograft environment were detected using a hypoxyprobe (HP2-100 Kit), which was purchased from Beijing Biolead Biology Sci & Tech Co., Ltd., according to the manufacturer's instructions. Pimonidazole hydrochloride (Hypoxyprobe™-1), which is reductively activated in hypoxic cells, was used to stain the hypoxic tissue. e antibody reagent MAb1 binds to activated pimonidazole, allowing its detection by immunochemical methods.

div.head: In vivo antitumour activity
div.p: Tumour-bearing mice were treated with drugs on days 10, 13, 16, 19 and 22. Bioluminescence imaging was performed on days 7, 14, 21, and 28 after inoculation to monitor intracranial tumour growth.
e body weight of each mouse was recorded every 2 days after the treatment.

e mice were sacrificed when they exhibited hemiplegia, listlessness, cachexia, or other neurological symptoms. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were plotted to show the survival time. Seven days after the last treatment, three mice from each group were euthanized, and the tumour tissues were used to measure the level of YAP.

div.head: Biological safety of AMVY@NPs
div.p: Seven days after the last treatment, the heart, liver, spleen, lungs and kidneys of the tumour-bearing mice were collected and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde.

ese major organs were made into paraffin sections and stained with H&E to observe the biological safety of the drugs. In addition, blood biochemical markers (alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine (CREA)) and routine blood profiles (red blood cells (RBCs) and white blood cells (WBCs)) were detected.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: e results are representative of experiments repeated at least three times and are presented as the mean ± SD. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to analyse multiple groups, followed by Dunnett's t test for post hoc pairwise comparisons. Overall survival curves were drawn via the Kaplan-Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. P values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001).

div.head: Results and discussion
div.p: Synthesis and characterization of AMVY@NPs e construction of polymetronidazole was confirmed by 1 H NMR, which revealed all of the characteristic peaks and integration values (Figure S1). Polymetronidazole, VP, siYAP, DOTAP, DSPE-PEG 2000 , lecithin and DSPE-PEG 2000 -Angiopep-2 were subsequently used to construct AMVY@NPs via the self-assembly method shown in Fig. 2A. In addition, to detect the hypoxia-responsive ability of AMVY@NPs, PLGA, an FDA-approved polymer material [38], was used to construct APVY@NPs as a control. To examine the synergistic effect of siYAP and VP on glioma growth, AMVY@NPs, AM@NPs (with siRNA and VP), AMY@NPs (loading siYAP only) and AMV@NPs (loading VP only) were synthesized as control groups.

As measured by dynamic light scattering (DLS), the hydrodynamic diameters of AM@NPs, AMY@NPs, AMV@NPs APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs were 97.9, 122, 118.6, 98.1 and 100.9 nm, respectively (Fig. 2B). e polydispersity indices (PDIs) of AM@NPs, AMY@NPs, AMV@NPs, APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs were all less than 0.3 (Figure S2B). e size and homogeneous spherical morphology of the nanoparticles were confirmed via TEM (Fig. 2C & Figure S2C). ese results revealed that the AMVY@NPs are small in size and have a spherical structure. Agarose gel electrophoresis revealed that siYAP was completely adsorbed by DOTAP when the N/P ratio was 7:1 (Fig. 2D, upper). After incubation of AMVY@NPs in heparin, which competitively adsorbs on the surface of liposomes through electrostatic action, siYAP could still be observed when the N/P ratio was 9:1, indicating that siYAP was loaded onto AMVY@NPs via electrostatic interactions (Fig. 2D bottom). Moreover, compared with that of AM@NPs, the zeta potential of siYAP-loaded AMY@NPs and AMVY@NPs clearly decreased (Figure S2D), suggesting that siYAP was successfully loaded onto cationic AMY@NPs and AMVY@ NPs. On the basis of the concentration-absorbance curve of VP (Figure S2E), the loading efficiency of VP was 80% in AMVY@NPs. In addition, in a simulated blood environment (DMEM containing 10% foetal bovine serum), the size and PDI of AMVY@NPs showed minimal changes over 5 consecutive days, suggesting the good stability of AMVY@NPs (Fig. 2E).

According to the properties of polymetronidazole, hydrophobic ImNO 2 can be converted to hydrophilic ImNH 2 under hypoxic conditions, releasing the encapsulated drug [39]. e release of VP and siYAP was detected to reflect the ability of AMVY@NPs to respond to hypoxia. Compared with only 40% under normoxic conditions, the amount of VP released from AMVY@NPs under hypoxic conditions reached 93% at 14 h (Fig. 2F). In contrast, the amount of VP released from APVY@ NPs was not significantly different under normoxic and hypoxic conditions (Fig. 2F). Similarly, the percentage of siYAP released from AMVY@NPs was 30% and 70% at 14 h under normoxic and hypoxic conditions, respectively (Fig. 2G). However, the amount of siYAP released from APVY@NPs was not significantly different under normoxic and hypoxic conditions (Fig. 2G).
is result revealed that AMVY@NPs could release more drugs under hypoxic conditions, which may be attributed to the hypoxic response of polymetronidazole.

As shown in Fig. 2H, the characteristic absorption peak of polymetronidazole in AMVY@NPs at 325 nm disappeared under hypoxic conditions. Furthermore, as determined by DLS or TEM, the diameter of AMVY@NPs became larger and more irregular under hypoxic conditions than that under normoxic conditions (Fig. 2I&J). However, the diameter of the APVY@NPs did not differ under normoxic and hypoxic conditions. ese results revealed that AMVY@NPs with hypoxia-responsive ability were successfully constructed.

div.head: In vitro tumour targeting and YAP inhibition effects of AMVY@NPs
div.p: Next, the noncytotoxic properties of AM@NPs and AP@ NPs (without siYAP or VP) were confirmed in HA1800, U87, U251, and GBM cells (Figure S3A). An in vitro BBB model in which HA1800 cells were mixed with bEnd.3 cells in the upper chamber and U87 cells in the lower Fig. 2 Characterization of AMVY@NPs A Schematic illustration of synthesis steps of AMVY@NPs. B Hydrodynamic diameters of AM@NPs, AMY@NPs, AMV@NPs, APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs. C TEM images of AMVY@NPs. Scale bare: 100 nm. D Agarose gel retardation assay for N/P with various ratios of DOTAP to siYAP under normal and heparin conditions. E Size and PDI of AMVY@NPs in DMEM containing 10% FBS during 5 consecutive days. F VP released from APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs under hypoxic and normoxic conditions. G siYAP released from APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs under hypoxic and normoxic conditions. H Absorption spectra of APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs under hypoxic and normoxic conditions for 4 h. I Hydrodynamic diameters of APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs under hypoxic and normoxic conditions. J TEM images of APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs under hypoxic and normoxic conditions. Scale bare: 100 nm chamber (Fig. 3A) was generated to evaluate the permeability of AMVY@NPs. As shown in Fig. 3B&C, the number of Cy5-positive cells in the AMCy5-siYAP@NPs group was much greater than that in the free Cy5-siYAP and MCy5-siYAP@NPs groups, suggesting the greater permeability of AMCy5-siYAP@NPs. Before nanoparticles act on glioma cells, they need to be taken up by the cells and escape from the lysosomes [40]. As shown in Figure S3B&C and Fig. 3D, AMCy5-siYAP@NPs were better taken up by glioma cells at 4 h (Figure S3B&C) and escaped from the lysosome at 8 h (Fig. 3D). is result confirmed that the siYAP carried by AMVY@NPs could not be degraded by lysosomes and therefore could subsequently exert an inhibitory effect on gliomas. ereafter, we evaluated the ability of AMVY@NPs to inhibit YAP on glioma cells. As shown in Figure S3D and S3E, compared with the PBS group, the mRNA level of YAP in U87 and U251 cells was reduced to approximately 40% after AMY@NPs, APVY@NPs and AMVY@NPs treatment in normoxia. However, under hypoxia, the mRNA level of YAP in U87 cells was reduced to 20%, and that in U251 cells was reduced to 12% both after AMY@ NP and AMVY@NPs treatment, whereas that in U87 and U251 cells was still reduced to 40% after APVY@ NPs treatment (Fig. 3E and F), indicating that AMVY@ NPs effectively respond to hypoxia. erefore, we proceeded with the subsequent in vitro experiments under hypoxic conditions.

Since some studies reported that, in addition to blocking the interaction of YAP and TEAD [41], VP could also reduce the protein level of YAP [11,14], we further evaluated the ability of AMVY@NPs to inhibit YAP at the protein level under hypoxia. As shown in Fig. 3G and J, compared with the free siYAP + VP group, AMVY@NPs significantly decreased the protein levels of YAP and its target genes (AXL and CTGF) in U87 and U251 cells. Notably, compared with APVY@NPs, AMVY@NPs more effectively inhibited YAP, AXL and CTGF (Fig. 3H-J), which may be due to the increased release of siYAP and VP in the hypoxic environment. Interestingly, AMVY@ NPs had a greater effect on YAP inhibition than AMY@ NPs and AMV@NPs did, suggesting that the siRNA and VP released from AMVY@NPs synergistically inhibited the protein level of YAP.

div.head: In vitro anti-cancer effect of AMVY@NPs
div.p: Next, the effect of AMVY@NPs on the proliferation of U87 cells in vitro was investigated via a CCK-8 assay. As shown in Fig. 4A, the viability of U87 cells decreased by 85% after AMVY@NPs treatment, which was much greater than that of any other group (AMY@NPs: 70%, AMV@NPs: 66% and APVY@NPs: 56%). Consistently, AMVY@NPs had a similar inhibitory effect on U251 glioma cells, as determined by both the CCK-8 assay (Fig. 4A bottom) and the colony formation assay (Fig. 4B&C). In addition, after various treatments, glioma cells were stained with AM/PI to distinguish live (green fluorescence) and dead (red fluorescence) cells. As shown in Fig. 4D and E, compared with the other treatments, AMVY@NPs treatment caused more cancer cell death. Furthermore, AMVY@NPs significantly inhibited the migration ability of glioma cells (Figure S4 A&B). Notably, in all of the above assays, siYAP and VP released from AMVY@NPs synergistically inhibited glioma cell growth and migration.

Considering that overexpression of YAP promotes the stemness of GSCs, leading to cancer progression and therapeutic resistance [42,43], we explored the influence of AMVY@NPs on the stemness of GSCs. After the GSCs were successfully identified by costaining for nestin and CD133, two well-known molecular markers of GSCs (Figure S4C), we performed a tumour sphere formation assay and found that AMVY@NPs significantly inhibited the sphere number of GSCs, which was greater than that of any other drugs (Fig. 4F and G). In addition, in the limited dilution assay, AMVY@NPs had the greatest inhibitory effect on the self-renewal potential of GSCs, indicating that AMVY@NPs inhibited the stemness of GSCs and were the most potent drug (Fig. 4H). Together, the above findings demonstrate that AMVY@NPs exhibit efficient anti-proliferative effects on both glioma cells and GSCs via synergistic inhibition of YAP by siYAP and VP.

div.head: In vivo GBM targeting and distribution profiles of AMVY@ NPs
div.p: To reveal the potential anti-GBM ability of AMVY@ NPs in vivo, we first examined the ability of AMVY@ NPs to target GBM and its distribution by using AMCy5-siYAP@NPs, which are similar in size to AMVY@NPs (Figure S5A&B). We generated an orthotopic glioma model by injecting U87-GFP-Luci + cells into the right striatum of nude mice, which was confirmed by in vivo bioluminescence imaging on day 7 (Fig. 5A). After U87-GFP-Luci + tumour-bearing mice were treated with free Cy5-siYAP, MCy5-siYAP@NPs or AMCy5-siYAP@NPs through the tail vein on day 10, the distribution of Cy5-siYAP was observed by in vivo bioluminescence imaging at different time points. As shown in Fig. 5B&C, after AMCy5-siYAP@NPs treatment, Cy5-siYAP fluorescence appeared in glioma at 1 h and gradually increased, indicating that AMCy5-siYAP@NPs crossed the BBB and entered tumour tissues more than free Cy5-siYAP or MCy5-siYAP@NPs did (Fig. 5B&C). Interestingly, the Cy5-siYAP fluorescence intensity could still be observed at the tumour site at 24 h after AMCy5-siYAP@NPs administration. In addition, examination of ex vivo images (Fig. 5D&E) and Cy5-siYAP fluorescence intensity in tumour slices (Fig. 5F&G) revealed that the AMCy5-siYAP@NPs group presented the highest Cy5-siYAP fluorescence in tumours among the three groups, further indicating that AMCy5-siYAP@NPs have the highest GBM-targeting ability.

e pharmacokinetic profiles of AMCy5-siYAP@NPs were subsequently analysed to evaluate their metabolic behaviour in vivo. On the basis of the concentration-fluorescence curve of Cy5-siYAP (Figure S5C), we dynamically measured the level of Cy5-siYAP fluorescence in the blood of mice following the injection of AMCy5-siYAP@ NPs. Mice that received an injection of free Cy5-siYAP or MCy5-siYAP@NPs were used as controls. Figure 5H shows that the half-life of the free Cy5-siYAP group was 1.5 h, whereas those of the MCy5-siYAP@NPs and AMCy5-siYAP@NPs groups were effectively prolonged to approximately 5 h, indicating that AMVY@NPs presented better stability, which may prolong the presence of siYAP and VP in the body. div.head: In vivo therapeutic effects of AMVY@NPs
div.p: We demonstrated that AMVY@NPs can release more drugs under hypoxic conditions (Fig. 2F&G). us, hypoxic conditions are important for the treatment of GBM with AMVY@NPs. We detected hypoxic conditions in the xenograft environment by using a hypoxyprobe, and the anoxia in the tumour tissue was clearly observed (Figure S6A, green). On the basis of the above results, we investigated the anti-GBM effect of AMVY@ NPs (VP: 10 mg/kg, siYAP: 0.25 mg/kg, five injections total) on orthotopic U87-luc + gliomas (Fig. 6A). e PBS, free VP, free siYAP, free VP + siYAP, AMY@NPs, AMV@ NPs, and APVY@NPs groups were used as controls. e antitumour effect was monitored via in vivo bioluminescence imaging at 7, 14, 21, and 28 days after U87-luc + cell implantation. As shown in Fig. 6B and C, compared with the free siYAP + VP group, the AMVY@NPs group presented weaker bioluminescence (a smaller tumour size), revealing the advantages of nanomedicine. Moreover, the bioluminescence of the AMVY@NPs group was weaker than that of the APVY@NPs group, which may be due to the increased release of siRNA and VP in the anoxic environment. Additionally, AMVY@NPs-treated mice presented the smallest tumour size according to H&E staining of the brain sections (Figure S6A). Kaplan-Meier survival curves revealed that tumour-bearing mice treated with AMVY@NPs presented the longest survival time (Fig. 6D). e body weights of the tumour-bearing mice treated with AMVY@NPs were relatively stable (Figure S6B).

ese results indicate that AMVY@NPs have significant antitumour effects. Notably, compared with AMY@NPs-or AMV@NPs-treated mice, tumourbearing mice treated with AMVY@NPs had smaller tumours and longer survival times, suggesting the synergistic effect of siYAP and VP (Fig. 6B-D).

To further explore the mechanism by which AMVY@ NPs inhibit tumour growth in vivo, the expression of YAP and its target genes AXL and CTGF in xenografts was detected via western blotting. As shown in Fig. 6E-H, compared with those in the free siYAP + VP group, the protein levels of YAP, AXL and CTGF in the AMVY@ NPs group were significantly lower, indicating the benefit of delivery by nanomedicine. In addition, the levels of YAP, AXL and CTGF in the AMVY@NPs group were lower than those in the APVY@NPs group, indicating that AMVY@NPs had the advantage of a hypoxia response in tumour tissue. Furthermore, AMVY@NPs had a stronger inhibitory effect than AMV@NPs or AMY@NPs did, suggesting that AMVY@NPs exhibited obvious antitumour ability, which was attributed to the synergistic inhibition of YAP by siRNA and VP.

Although AMVY@NPs had a stronger anti-GBM effect than any other agent did, AMVY@NPs did not kill all of the GBM cells. erefore, to produce a better therapeutic effect on GBM, we could enhance the targeting efficacy of nanoparticles with better guide molecules or improve the responsive release of drugs in the tumour microenvironment by using pH-or redox reactant-sensitive materials combined with polymetronidazole [44]. is is interesting work for the future.

div.head: Biological safety of AMVY@NPs
div.p: To evaluate the biological safety of AMVY@NPs in vivo, the main organs (including the heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney) of tumour-bearing mice were dissected 7 days after AMVY@NPs treatment and stained with H&E. As shown in Fig. 7A, the major organs of tumour-bearing mice treated with AMVY@NPs presented no obvious changes in morphology, revealing that AMVY@NPs have improved biological safety. Moreover, the blood of the mice was collected 7 days after the different treatments to detect blood biochemical markers (ALT, AST, BUN, and CREA) and routine profiles (RBCs and WBCs). e results were all within the normal range (Fig. 7B-G), indicating that the liposomes had no noticeable toxicity.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We successfully synthesized a stepwise-targeting and hypoxia-responsive liposome AMVY@NPs carrying siYAP and VP for glioblastoma therapy. In body fluid, the AMVY@NPs displayed a high degree of stability, ensuring the long cycle time required for tumour targeting. Under the guidance of A2, AMVY@NPs specifically crossed the BBB and then accumulated in the GBM.
